**Before the appointment**
- Add the appointment date in the 'Appointment' tab. MenoMap shows how ready your notes are and what might make them stronger.
- Choose the topics and questions most important to you. Stick to three or four.
- Create your notes for the last 30 or 90 days. And make sure your medication list is up to date.

**During the appointment**
- Hand over or show the first page. It is designed to be read in under a minute: the counts, averages, heat calendar and your questions.
- Start with the question most important to you.
- If your doctor speaks another language, you can create the notes in that language.

**What these notes are, and what they are not**

They are a summary of what you entered, plus any data you chose to bring in from the Health app. They are not a diagnosis nor a complete medical record, and any patterns in them are an observation of coincidence (co-occurrence), not proof of cause. Your doctor may ask questions the notes don't answer, and that is normal.

**After the appointment**

Add any new medication with its start date. After a few weeks, MenoMap can show your entries before and after starting, which makes your next review easier.
backTranslations.42:
**Menopause** is a single point in time: the day when 12 consecutive months without a period are completed, when there is no other explanation for that (such as pregnancy, certain medications or surgery). In many countries it happens on average in the early fifties, but occurring any time between the mid-forties and mid-fifties is common.

**Perimenopause** is the years leading up to that point. Hormone levels rise and fall irregularly, so the cycle may become irregular, heavier, lighter, closer together, or further apart. Many of the changes people associate with menopause, such as hot flashes, night sweats, sleep changes and mood changes, often begin in this period, while periods are still continuing. This period may last a few years or much longer, and it differs from one person to another.

**Postmenopause** is everything that follows the twelve-month mark. Some symptoms calm down over time, and some may continue for years.

Menopause can also occur early because of surgery to remove the ovaries, certain cancer treatments, or other health conditions. Menopause before age forty is sometimes called premature ovarian insufficiency, and it is worth discussing with a doctor.

**How it is recognized.** For many people over 45, doctors recognize perimenopause or menopause from your health history and symptoms. Blood tests are not always necessary, because hormone levels fluctuate from day to day. They are more likely to be used when the person is younger or the picture is unclear.

**What MenoMap does and does not do.** MenoMap cannot tell you which stage you are in. What it can do is keep an honest record of what you notice: waves, sleep, mood and treatment, so that you and your doctor look at the same picture.

backTranslations.162:
Doctors call hot flashes and night sweats **vasomotor symptoms**. A hot flash is a sudden wave of heat, often in the face, neck and chest, sometimes accompanied by redness, sweating, a racing heartbeat, or chills afterward. A night sweat is the same thing during sleep, and it may be severe enough to wake you or soak your sheets.

They are among the most common changes in the perimenopausal period. Some people get a few mild flashes, while others get many flashes a day that disrupt work and sleep. In some people they fade within a few years, and in others they continue much longer.

**What may make them more likely.** People often notice patterns linked to alcohol, caffeine, spicy food, hot rooms, stress and heavy covers. This varies a lot from person to person, which is why tracking your own tags may be more useful than a generic list.

**There are other causes.** Flushing and sweating can also result from thyroid problems, infection, certain medications, anxiety, or other conditions. If your symptoms don't fit the usual pattern, or are accompanied by weight loss, fever or feeling unwell, mention it to the doctor.

**Describing them precisely.** Details useful for the appointment:
- how many per day and at night, roughly
- how severe and how long they last
- what they interrupt: sleep, work, conversations, exercise
- what seems to precede them
- what you have tried, and whether it changed anything

MenoMap's wave button and the ability to log later are there to record exactly this without much effort.

**Help is available.** There are hormonal and non-hormonal treatment options, in addition to practical approaches. Which of them suits you is a conversation you have with the doctor.

backTranslations.291:
Hormone therapy (often called HRT or MHT) replaces part of the estrogen that the body produces less of in the perimenopausal period. Major medical guidelines describe it as an effective treatment for hot flashes and night sweats in many people, and it may help with other symptoms too.

**It comes in different forms:** patches, gel, sprays, tablets, and low-dose vaginal preparations for local symptoms such as dryness. Those who still have a uterus are usually prescribed progesterone alongside estrogen to protect the uterine lining.

**Benefits and risks differ from person to person:** age, time since periods stopped, personal and family history (such as breast cancer, blood clots, stroke or heart disease), the type of treatment and how it is taken. That is why it is a decision made with a doctor who knows your health history, and not something an app can decide.

**Questions people often ask:**
- Is hormone therapy a suitable option for me, and why or why not?
- What type and form do you suggest, and why?
- What benefits can I expect, and after how long?
- What are my specific risks, and how do they compare with no treatment?
- What should I watch for, and when do we review it?

**If you are already taking it,** log it in MenoMap (My profile > Medications). MenoMap will show your waves before you started and after, as an observation of coincidence and not proof, so that you have something concrete to discuss at the review.

MenoMap never suggests starting, stopping or changing a medication.

backTranslations.293:
Hormone therapy is not suitable for everyone, and some people simply prefer other approaches. There are several approaches.

**Prescription options.** Some non-hormonal medications have evidence that they reduce hot flashes. They include medications originally developed for other conditions, and a newer class designed specifically for hot flashes. Each has its benefits, side effects and interactions, so the doctor can help you weigh them.

**Talk therapy and mind-body approaches.** Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) adapted for menopause has evidence that it makes hot flashes and night sweats less bothersome and improves sleep. Clinical hypnosis has also been studied.

**Practical changes people find helpful:**
- clothing layers that can be removed quickly
- a fan on the desk and beside the bed
- a cooler bedroom and well-ventilated covers
- noticing and reducing personal triggers (MenoMap's tags and experiments help with this)
- regular physical activity and a steady sleep routine

**Supplements and herbal products.** Evidence is conflicting or limited for many of them, their quality varies, and some interact with other medications. Tell your doctor or pharmacist everything you take, including products sold without a prescription.

**Try one change at a time.** MenoMap's two-week experiments compare your entries before the change and during it, and this is easier to judge than just a feeling.

backTranslations.416:
Most appointments are short, and it is hard to remember a month of nights on the spot. People tend to remember the last days or the worst days. A simple log fills this gap.

**What a symptom log gives your doctor:**
- how often symptoms happen and how severe they are, not just that they happen
- whether things are improving, worsening or staying the same
- what was going on around them: sleep, alcohol, stress, medications
- a starting point for comparison if you try a treatment

**Keep it light.** A log is only useful if you keep at it. MenoMap is designed around a one-tap wave button and an evening log of four questions, so it takes seconds, not a whole notebook.

**Two weeks is a good start.** Entries from two to four weeks usually show a clearer picture than one bad week.

**Bring your questions too.** Write down what matters most to you: the symptom that bothers you most, what you want to try or avoid, anything that worries you. MenoMap's 'Appointment' tab helps you choose questions and prints them with your notes.

backTranslations.479:
After 12 months without a period, **a doctor should check any vaginal bleeding**, even if it happened only once, and even if it was just spotting or light pink or brown discharge.

Most of the time the cause turns out not to be serious. Thinning of the vaginal or uterine lining is common, for example. But bleeding after menopause can sometimes be an early sign of a condition that is much easier to treat if found early. That is why general health guidelines advise checking it rather than waiting.

**If you are taking hormone therapy,** some bleeding patterns may be expected, depending on the type you take. But bleeding that is unexpected with your treatment, heavier than usual, or occurring at the wrong time should also be checked.

**What you do:**
- Contact your doctor or the health service and say you had bleeding after menopause.
- Note the date, the amount, and anything else you noticed. MenoMap can save that for you (My profile > Cycle).

MenoMap cannot tell you why the bleeding happened. It will remind you to check it and include it in your appointment notes.

backTranslations.529:
Lack of sleep is one of the most common complaints in midlife, and it rarely has a single cause.

**Night sweats** can wake you directly, or leave you very hot or wet so you can't get back to sleep.

**Other common factors:**
- needing to urinate at night
- anxiety or racing thoughts
- alcohol, which may help you fall asleep but tends to fragment the second half of the night
- caffeine late in the day
- pain, restless legs, or a partner's snoring
- snoring or pauses in breathing, which may be a sign of sleep apnea (worth mentioning, especially if you feel very sleepy during the day)

**What usually helps people.** A cool, dark room; well-ventilated covers and clothing layers that can be removed; a fixed wake-up time; reducing alcohol near bedtime. And cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is a structured, well-studied approach, and many doctors can refer you to it.

**What to track.** For a week or two, note your sleep rating, night waves, alcohol, and late caffeine. MenoMap's evening log and wave log do this in a few taps. And if you use an Apple Watch, MenoMap can show your sleep and wrist temperature from the Health app alongside night sweats, as context rather than explanation.

**When to get checked.** Talk to a doctor if lack of sleep affects your safety (such as driving), your mood, or your daily life, or if you notice pauses in your breathing or gasping at night.
